tradition.name: Dutch running hand (lopende hand)
tradition.notes: The everyday Dutch hand of the Golden Age, a gothic cursive related to secretary and Kurrent; hard for today's readers. Near-upright with a tiny x-height under tall looped or back-leaning ascenders; minims joined foot-to-head (n reads like u), secretary e laid flat, h and z sweeping below the line, figure-of-eight g, long ſ. Letters keep the plate's own hairline entries and exits; flourished capitals.

source.name: Maria Strick, Schat oft voorbeelt (1618), sheet 31
source.credit: Maria Strick (1577–after 1631), Schat oft voorbeelt ende verthooninge van verscheyden geschriften (Rotterdam, 1618), engraved by Hans Strick; sheet 31, 'Fondament vande Loopende Letter' and the Nederlandtsche Capitalen. Rijksmuseum, Amsterdam, BI-1885-1328-31; Public Domain Mark

glyphs.note: bowl counter-clockwise from its top right, then the stem entered by a short hairline ear from the upper right (alpha-like), exit hairline
looped ascender: upstroke on the right, down the stem, bowl clockwise, closed by a bar that crosses the stem at x-height
the top arm runs out as a long hairline at x-height (the connector of the running hand)
uncial d: small cup, up the back-leaning ascender (hairline), down it as the shaded stroke, exit; one gesture
looped d: hook, up the right side into a tall loop leaning back, down crossing near the baseline, exit
secretary (reversed) e laid flat: the low bowl stroke rising into a small eye at the top right, hairline exit; the plate's long lead-in wave shortened
figure-of-eight g: small head, the descender loops back up across itself; written larger on the plate, scaled by its own head
secretary h: hooked ascender down to the x-height, then the limb swings right and below the baseline and sweeps back left under the previous letter
